title: Two fingers, not every pair
hook: Eight numbers make 28 pairs. A sorted list lets you skip most of them.

knows: binary search halves a sorted list (binary-search)
doesNotKnow: that a sorted list lets one check rule out a whole row of pairs

misconception: To find two numbers that add to a target you must try every pair.
objective: The learner can explain that on a sorted list a sum that is too small rules out the smaller number with every partner, so moving one finger per check finds a pair in at most n - 1 sums (7 for 8 numbers) instead of 28.

claims.source: 8 x 7 / 2 = 28; the triangle grid on the stage draws all 28.

claims.text: On 1 3 4 6 8 11 13 15 with target 19, the two-finger rule checks 1 + 15 = 16, 3 + 15 = 18, then 4 + 15 = 19: three sums, ruling out 13 of the 28 pairs without looking at them.
claims.source: Builder's node script (scratchpad checks/all.mjs) runs the rule: 3 checks for 19. Ruled-out count: rows 1 (7 pairs) and 3 (6 pairs) = 13.

claims.text: Because the list is sorted, if 1 + 15 is too small then 1 is too small with every partner.
claims.source: 15 is the largest number, so 1 + x <= 1 + 15 < 19 for every x in the list.

claims.text: Each sum moves a finger one step inward, so 8 numbers need at most 7 sums.
claims.source: Derivation: the gap j - i starts at 7 and falls by 1 per check, stopping at 0. Builder's node script over every target 0..35 on this list: maximum 7 checks.

claims.text: The rule never skips a pair that adds to the target.
claims.source: Derivation: a pair is ruled out only when its row or column is shown too small or too big with the extreme partner (see c3). Problem as CLRS 3rd ed. exercise 2.3-7 (pair summing to x in a set).

recall.question: A sorted list has 100 numbers. With one finger at each end, moving the left one right when the sum is too small and the right one left when too big, at most how many sums do you check?
recall.why: Each sum moves one finger one step inward, so the gap of 99 closes in at most 99 checks. 4,950 is the number of pairs.
